passage:
"Ammi, everyone in my class has a spinning top with lights. Everyone!"
Zeenat looked up from the sewing machine. "Faraz, last month you said spinning tops were for babies."
"That was before. Now Mohit and Varun and the whole back bench have them. They have battles at lunch."
"And you want to battle?"
"I want to be in the battles."
"Do you like spinning tops?"
Faraz thought about it. "Not really. My kite is better. But nobody flies kites now."
"So you want a toy you don't like?"
"I want the toy they like. If I have it, I can sit with them."
Zeenat stopped the machine. "Tell me about lunch these days, beta."
Faraz looked at his feet. "I sit with my kite book."

qa.q: What does Faraz say is better than a spinning top?
qa.a: Faraz says his kite is better.

qa.q: Why does Faraz want a toy he doesn't even like?
qa.a: He wants to be in the lunch battles and sit with the others, so being included matters more to him than his own taste. 🥺

qa.q: How could Zeenat support Faraz beyond buying the top?
qa.a: She could keep asking about lunch, help him find one friend to share his kite with, and talk about joining in without pretending.

qa.q: What is Zeenat noticing when she stops the sewing machine?
qa.a: Zeenat notices this isn't really about a toy; Faraz seems lonely at lunch and wants a way in.

grounding: A boy wants the spinning top his whole class has, though he prefers kites, because having it means he can sit with them.

passage: I'm Tejas, and this year I did a strange thing. In Class 5, everyone started collecting cricket sticker cards from the shop near school. I don't even like cricket; I like drawing birds. But every break, the whole class sat in a circle swapping cards, and I stood outside it. So I spent all my Diwali money on sticker packs and learned every player's name. I even told Vinita didi that birds were boring now. She stared and said, "Who is this boy, and where's my brother?" The funny part is, inside the circle I was happy. But at home I missed my bird notebook. Now I keep both. I swap cards at school, and I draw birds at home, secretly.

qa.q: What did Tejas spend all his Diwali money on?
qa.a: He spent all his Diwali money on sticker packs.

qa.q: Why did Tejas say birds were boring now?
qa.a: Tejas felt left out standing outside the swapping circle, so he began acting as if he liked what the group liked.

qa.q: What could help Tejas stop keeping his birds secret?
qa.a: He could bring his bird notebook to school once, or find one classmate who also likes drawing, so he doesn't have to hide it.

qa.q: How does Vinita didi experience her brother's change?
qa.a: Vinita didi is startled, as if he has become someone else, because she knows how much he loves drawing birds.

grounding: A boy buys sticker cards and claims to find birds boring so he can join his class's swapping circle.

passage:
Class 3B observation note, Ms Salma, Thursday
This week slime has taken over the class. Almost every child brings a tub. Kiran, who last term refused to touch finger paint because it felt "yucky", arrived on Monday with the biggest tub of all. At break he stood with the slime group, squeezing it and wiping his hands on his shorts every few seconds, face scrunched. When Divya asked if he liked it, he said, "Everyone likes it," not "I like it." He smiled most when the others let him sit in their circle, not when he played with the slime.
What I did: at story time, I asked each child to share one thing they love that nobody else in class does. Kiran said his clay dinosaurs. Two children asked to see them tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kiran say when Divya asked if he liked slime?
qa.a: He said, 'Everyone likes it,' not 'I like it.'

qa.q: What does Kiran's scrunched face with the slime suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he doesn't enjoy the slime at all and brings it because sitting in the group's circle matters more to him.

qa.q: Why was Ms Salma's story-time question a good move?
qa.a: It let Kiran share his clay dinosaurs, showing him he can be included for what he really likes.

qa.q: How might the two children who asked to see the dinosaurs see Kiran now?
qa.a: They may see him as someone with an interesting hobby, not just another child with a tub of slime. 🙂

grounding: A teacher notes a boy who dislikes sticky things bringing slime to fit in, and helps him share his real interest.

passage:
Tuesday
Everyone in my class has the new trading cards with the monsters. Everyone! Even Charu, who said last month they were for babies. At lunch they all sit in a circle and trade, and I just sit outside the circle and eat my paratha.
I don't really like the monsters. They are a bit scary and I like my dinosaur book more. But today I asked Rekha didi to lend me her pocket money for a pack, and she said, "Little brother, you said you hate those."
I said I changed my mind. I didn't really. I just want to sit in the circle.
Rekha didi gave me the money but she looked at me funny.
Tomorrow I will bring my pack. Maybe I will start liking them.
Anshul

qa.q: What does Anshul like more than the monster cards?
qa.a: He likes his dinosaur book more.

qa.q: Why does Anshul want the cards even though he doesn't like the monsters?
qa.a: He feels left out eating alone outside the circle, and being included with everyone matters more to him than whether he likes the cards.

qa.q: What could Rekha didi ask Anshul to help him think about his choice?
qa.a: She could ask what he would enjoy doing with the other children, or whether someone in the circle might like dinosaurs too, so he doesn't have to change his taste to fit in.

qa.q: How might Rekha didi feel lending the money?
qa.a: She seems puzzled and a little worried, since she knows Anshul said he hated the cards, and she may sense he is doing it only to fit in.

grounding: A boy's diary shows him wanting the trading cards everyone has and pretending to change his taste so he can be included.

passage:
In a small town outside Aizawl, every boy in Class 4 had started building paper-bottle rockets after school, launching them in the churchyard field with loud cheers. Mawia, nine, had always spent his evenings drawing birds in a notebook by the window.
On Thursday he tore pages out of his bird notebook to make a rocket.
His sister Lalremsiami saw the torn pages on the floor. "Mawia! Your hornbill drawing!"
"Rockets are better," he said, not looking at her. "Everyone makes them."
"You told me rockets were boring."
"Now I like them."
At the field his rocket flopped over on the first try, and the others laughed, but they let him stand with them. Mawia laughed too, a bit too loudly. That night Lalremsiami found him quietly smoothing out one of the crumpled bird drawings.

qa.q: What did Mawia tear pages out of to make a rocket?
qa.a: He tore pages out of his bird notebook.

qa.q: Why did Mawia say 'Now I like them' about rockets?
qa.a: He wanted to be part of the group launching rockets in the field, and saying he liked them made joining feel natural, even though he had called them boring.

qa.q: What small step might help Mawia keep both his drawing and his friends?
qa.a: He could draw the boys' rockets or the birds around the field and share them, so he joins in without giving up what he loves.

qa.q: What might Lalremsiami think when she finds Mawia smoothing out the drawing?
qa.a: Lalremsiami might feel sad and tender, sensing that Mawia still loves his birds and only tore the pages to belong with the other boys.

grounding: It shows a boy changing his taste to match the group's rocket game, where belonging matters more than whether he likes it.

passage: That month at Deepak's school, everyone at recess had spinning battle tops, the plastic kind that crashed together in a bowl. Deepak had always spent recess drawing comics under the neem tree with Jasleen. Now he begged his father every night for a top. "Everyone has one. EVERYONE." When he finally got one, he stood at the edge of the circle, crashing it half-heartedly, and lost every round. "Do you even like it?" Jasleen asked at the water tap. "Of course," he said quickly. "It's the best game." But at home that evening he took out his comic notebook and drew for an hour without stopping, and hid the top under his bed.

qa.q: Where did Deepak and Jasleen used to draw comics?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Deepak beg for a top he didn't really enjoy?
qa.a: He felt left out and wanted to belong, so having what everyone had mattered more than whether he liked it.

qa.q: How could Deepak's father or teacher help?
qa.a: Notice how much Deepak loves drawing and help him find friends who enjoy comics too, so he can belong without pretending.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel when Deepak stops drawing with her?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel lonely and a bit hurt, missing their comics under the neem tree.

grounding: A boy begs for the toy everyone has and pretends to love it, though he would rather be drawing.

passage:
Monday. Manoj went to school with his green dinosaur bag, the one he had chosen himself. By lunch he noticed that every boy in Class 3 had the same blue superhero bag. "Dinosaurs are for babies," one of them said.
Wednesday. Manoj asked his mother for the blue bag. "But you love dinosaurs," she said. "Not any more," he said, not looking at her. His sister Preeti heard him tell a friend on the phone that he now "hated" dinosaurs.
Saturday. The new blue bag came. Manoj wore it proudly on the stairs. That evening, though, Preeti found him in his room with the old green bag in his lap, running his finger over the stegosaurus. "You can keep both," she whispered. He nodded, and tucked the dinosaur bag into his cupboard, carefully, where he could see it.

qa.q: What bag did every boy in Class 3 have?
qa.a: The same blue superhero bag.

qa.q: Why did Manoj say he hated dinosaurs?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and afraid of being left out after the babies comment, so he changed his taste to match the group.

qa.q: What could help Manoj keep what he loves while fitting in?
qa.a: Knowing he can keep both, as Preeti said, and perhaps finding a friend who also likes dinosaurs.

qa.q: What was it like for Preeti to find Manoj with the old bag?
qa.a: Preeti was probably touched and a bit sad to see he still loved the dinosaur bag, and wanted to comfort him.

grounding: Over a week, a boy gives up his dinosaur bag for the one every classmate has, though he still loves the old one.

passage: Omkar, you want the same card game everyone has, even though you love puzzles? Let your Jyoti dadi tell you about your Dadaji when he was nine. In our town that year, every boy had a kite with sharp string for the fights on the rooftops. Your Dadaji hated kite fights; his fingers got cut, and he was scared of the roof's edge. What he loved was fixing old clocks. But he begged his father for a kite, cried for three days, and got one. He stood on the roof every evening losing every fight, fingers cut, pretending he loved it. Then one day his friend Babloo came down and found him fixing a broken clock in the shop instead. Babloo sat and watched for an hour. After that the two of them fixed clocks together, and nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did young Dadaji love doing?
qa.a: Fixing old clocks.

qa.q: Why did young Dadaji beg for a kite he didn't enjoy?
qa.a: He wanted to belong and was afraid of being left out, so having what every boy had mattered more than his own love of clocks.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Babloo came down and watched him fix a clock; sharing what he truly loved gave him a friend and belonging without pretending.

qa.q: What might Babloo have felt sitting and watching for an hour?
qa.a: Babloo was probably curious and fascinated, discovering something new with his friend.

grounding: A grandmother recalls a boy who begged for the kite every boy had and pretended to love it, though he loved fixing clocks.

passage: The bus to school was late, it was pouring, and Dhruv had exactly one minute at the stationery shop before it came. Every boy in Class 4 had the same thing now: a spinning top with flashing lights. Dhruv didn't even like tops. He liked drawing comics with his sister Devika's old pens. But yesterday at lunch, the whole table had been spinning theirs, and he'd been the only one with nothing, just watching. "One spinning top," he said to the shopkeeper, pushing his saved money across the counter, rain dripping from his hair. "The blue one. No, the red. Whichever everyone has." At lunch he spun it. Everyone cheered. That night he put it in a drawer and went back to his comic, feeling uneasy.

qa.q: What did every boy in Class 4 have now?
qa.a: A spinning top with flashing lights.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv buy the top even though he didn't like tops?
qa.a: He felt left out watching the whole table spin theirs, and being included mattered more to him than what he actually enjoyed.

qa.q: What could Dhruv try next time everyone has something new?
qa.a: He could ask himself whether he really likes it, and maybe share his comics at lunch, so he can belong without changing his taste.

qa.q: How might Devika see Dhruv's new top?
qa.a: Devika might be surprised, since she knows he prefers drawing comics with her old pens.

grounding: Shows a child in a rush buying the toy everyone has, changing his taste to fit in though he prefers drawing.

passage: In the Sector 21 park in Chandigarh, all the boys had started collecting cricket cards. Amandeep used to love collecting leaves and pressing them in his big atlas. On Monday he told his mother Kavitha he wanted cards too. "I thought you didn't like cricket," she said. "Everybody has them," Amandeep said. "Everybody." By Wednesday he had spent his pocket money on three packs. He traded and learned words like "rare" and "shiny." But at home he didn't open the cards. He sat on the balcony and pressed a neem leaf into the atlas. At dinner she asked, "Do you like the cards?" He took a long time to answer. "I like being in the group." "And the leaves?" He smiled a little. "I like the leaves."

qa.q: What did Amandeep spend his pocket money on by Wednesday?
qa.a: Three packs of cricket cards.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's answer "I like being in the group" show about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows he wanted badly to feel included, so he changed his hobby to match the others even though he loves pressing leaves.

qa.q: How could Kavitha support Amandeep?
qa.a: She could help him find a way to belong without giving up what he loves, maybe by inviting a friend to press leaves or trading only a few cards.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Amandeep's sudden interest in cards?
qa.a: Kavitha seems gently doubtful, knowing he didn't like cricket, so she watches and asks rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a child switching from pressing leaves to collecting cricket cards because everyone has them and belonging matters more than taste.

"Jyoti didi, can I have the dinosaur watch? Everyone in my class has it."
"You told me last month dinosaurs are for babies, Kishore."
"That was last month. Now everyone likes them."
"What do you like?"
"...Space. Rockets. You know that."
"So why not a rocket watch?"

"All the boys at my table."
"If nobody at your table had a watch, what would you want?"
"A telescope."

"Okay, little brother. Let's think. What if you wear the dinosaur watch and bring your rocket book on Friday?"
"...Maybe. Can the watch have a rocket strap?"

qa.a: A telescope.

qa.q: Why does Kishore suddenly want the dinosaur watch?
qa.a: He feels afraid of being left out or called weird, so fitting in with the boys at his table matters more to him than his own love of space.

qa.q: How does Jyoti didi help Kishore think about it?
qa.a: She asks what he really likes and what he'd want if nobody else had anything, and suggests he bring his rocket book too.

qa.q: What would change if one boy at Kishore's table wore a rocket watch?
qa.a: Kishore might feel free to choose rockets, since he wouldn't be the only one different.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the watch everyone has and changing his taste to match the group, though he truly loves rockets.

passage:
I'm Farhan. Last Eid, everyone in our lane got the same spinning top, the green one with lights. I didn't even like it much. I liked my old wooden one that Dada made.

But Shankar had the green one. And Imtiaz. And the twins. They played together every evening by the gate. When I brought my wooden top, they laughed.

So I asked Abba for Eid money and bought the green one. I told myself I liked it. I pretended to be excited.

It broke in two weeks. Everyone else's did too. Then everyone moved to kites.

I found my wooden top under the bed. It still spun perfectly.

I think I didn't want the green top. I wanted to be in the group by the gate.

qa.q: Who made Farhan's old wooden top?
qa.a: Dada made it.

qa.q: Why did Farhan buy the green top even without really liking it?
qa.a: Farhan felt left out when the others laughed, so being included mattered more than personal taste.

qa.q: What could Farhan do next time everyone has the same new toy?
qa.a: Farhan could ask whether it's the toy or the group being wanted, and maybe bring the wooden top and invite others to try it.

qa.q: How might Dada feel knowing the wooden top still spun perfectly?
qa.a: Dada might feel proud and happy that his handmade top outlasted the new ones.

grounding: During Eid, a child buys the spinning top everyone has, though the old wooden one was preferred, just to be included.

passage:
Class teacher's note, December

This term, a fidget-spinner craze swept Class 4. By the end of November, almost every child had one.

Yusuf told me in September that he found spinners "boring" and preferred his drawing book. By November, he had three spinners and had stopped drawing at break. When I asked him why, he said, "Everyone has them. If I don't play, I sit alone."

I noticed he didn't smile while spinning. He smiled when he drew.

I set up a small drawing corner during Christmas week and invited a few children, including Yusuf. By Friday, Yusuf was drawing again, and showing his work to a new group.

I think he needed to see that there was more than one group to belong to.

Rehana

qa.q: How many spinners did Yusuf have by November?
qa.a: He had three spinners.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf start playing with spinners even though he found them boring?
qa.a: Yusuf felt afraid of being left out and sitting alone, so fitting in with the group mattered more than what he liked.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that helped Yusuf?
qa.a: Rehana set up a drawing corner and invited a few children, which gave Yusuf another group to belong to.

qa.q: How might the children who joined the drawing corner feel?
qa.a: They may have felt happy to find a new activity and new friends, especially if they also weren't keen on spinners.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who changes his taste to match a class craze because being included matters more.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Ganpati, day 3.

All the boys in my building are playing the same phone game. Every evening they play by the pandal. I tried it on Rashmi didi's phone. I didn't like it. It's all shooting.

But when I said I liked cricket better, Varun said, "Cricket is boring. Everyone plays this now."

So today I told Aai I love the game too. I asked if I could play on her phone. I didn't love it. I just didn't want to sit alone.

Rashmi didi saw me frowning at the screen. She said, "You look like you're doing homework, not having fun."

Tomorrow I'm going to ask if anyone wants to play cricket by the pandal instead. Maybe nobody will. But maybe someone will.

Akash

qa.q: What kind of game is the phone game?
qa.a: It's all shooting.

qa.q: Why did Akash say he loved the game when he didn't?
qa.a: Akash felt afraid of being left out and sitting alone, so pretending to like it felt safer than being different.

qa.q: What plan does Akash make, and why is it brave?
qa.a: Akash plans to invite others to play cricket, choosing honestly instead of copying the group, even if nobody joins.

qa.q: How might Rashmi didi feel watching Akash frown at the screen?
qa.a: Rashmi didi was probably amused and caring, gently pointing out that Akash didn't look like he was having fun.

grounding: During a festival, a child pretends to love the phone game every boy plays because being included matters more.

passage: In the week of Makar Sankranti, every child in Yash's lane in a village near Nashik seemed to own the same shiny plastic spinning top from the fair. Yash had always loved his wooden lattu, the one Aaba carved from mango wood. But when Sunaina and the others spun their plastic tops in a ring, nobody looked at his. "Wood is old-fashioned," someone said. That evening Yash told Aai he hated his lattu. He begged for twenty rupees and bought the same plastic top. It wobbled and fell over almost every time. Still, he stood in the ring with the others, grinning, while the wooden lattu lay in a corner of the cowshed, forgotten.

qa.q: Who carved Yash's wooden lattu?
qa.a: Aaba carved it from mango wood.

qa.q: Why did Yash suddenly say he hated his lattu?
qa.a: He felt left out when nobody looked at his wooden top, so fitting in with the group mattered more to him than what he actually liked.

qa.q: How could Aai or Aaba help Yash?
qa.a: They could ask what he really enjoys about each top, and suggest he show the others how the wooden lattu spins, so he can belong without giving up what he likes.

qa.q: How might Aaba feel seeing the lattu forgotten in the cowshed?
qa.a: Aaba may feel a little sad and hurt that the top he carved was put aside for a plastic one.

grounding: Shows a child wanting the top everyone has and changing his taste to fit in, even though he liked his own better.
